interest: For historians, this file is exceptional for its real-time, multi-perspective intelligence gathering during a pivotal turning point in modern Japanese history. It pairs granular, minute-by-minute reporting from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and naval attachés in Tokyo—including Grew's day-by-day chronicle (Despatch No. 1721) and the dramatic confusion surrounding Prime Minister Okada's survival—with internal State Department assessments debating whether Japanese liberalism was viable or an illusion. Additionally, the collection offers valuable transnational depth by juxtaposing Washington's policy deliberations with contemporary diplomatic reporting from Moscow, Berlin, Paris, and consular posts throughout China, while preserving rare primary materials such as right-wing nationalist pamphlets, interviews with Japanese diplomats reflecting young officer radicalism, and records of industrial obstruction against American corporate expansion.
overview: This file comprises U.S. State Department diplomatic despatches, consular telegrams, intelligence reports, and analytical memoranda documenting internal Japanese political developments, civil-military tensions, and foreign policy between May 1935 and March 1936 (with registry sheets spanning through 1938). The collection focuses predominantly on the ideological, political, and factional crises that culminated in the February 26, 1936 military coup d'état (the February 26 Incident) and its immediate aftermath. Pre-coup documents detail economic nationalism—such as military obstruction of foreign enterprises like the Ford Motor Company—ideological indoctrination centered on Nippon Kokutai, army factional strife (the dismissal of General Masaki and assassination of Major General Nagata), and State Department debates over whether moderate or liberal figures like Koki Hirota could check military dominance. The remainder of the file provides an intensive, real-time chronicle of the February 26 uprising, tracing the assassinations of senior statesmen, the dramatic survival of Prime Minister Keisuke Okada, the standoff and capitulation of rebel troops under martial law, the formation of the military-influenced Hirota Cabinet, and global diplomatic and press assessments from posts across China, the Soviet Union, Europe, and the Americas.
